item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Glaciology] According to the professor, what did the lake cores show about how long the 1870s advance lasted?
choices: It came as two pushes, separated by a lull long enough for soil to begin forming

item.passage: Transcript: The Vasslen glacier. First, the eighteen-seventies advance. The lake cores finally settle its length, and the answer is odd: two distinct pushes. Between them the ice withdrew, and it stayed back long enough for a thin soil to start forming on the fresh moraine. So it did not hold the valley throughout, and the whole affair was far too drawn out to fit inside ten years. The maps that stretch it toward fifty years are simply misdated. Now the present advance, and here is my central point: this is a change at the bed, not in the budget. The surveys find no gain in mass anywhere on the glacier; the ice is simply sliding faster over its bed. No bulge is traveling down the ice from snowy winters past, the soundings off the front show clean deep water with nothing building there, and the tributary arms are as stagnant as ever. Faster sliding, same glacier. What next? The team means to winter over — keeping the station manned through the dark months for the first time. The stake line will stay where it is, the nineteen thirty-eight ridge stations were re-photographed two summers ago, and there will be no camera on the spur, which cannot be serviced in winter. Last, the Ravnas farm. From its yard, someone drew the glacier in seventeen ninety-four — the earliest picture of the ice that we possess. The farm's account books are lost, no grazing quarrel there ever came to law, and the family never sold so much as a block of ice. But that sketch is where the whole record begins.

item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Economic History] Why does the professor work through a single page of the Ostrand ledgers in class?
choices: To show the notation that has to be decoded before any of the totals can be used
To show how one entry can be followed out into the firm's correspondence
To show the change of hand that marks where the founder's son took over the books

item.passage: Transcript: Every year I put one page of the Ostrand ledgers on screen, for the same reason: there, in a single column, barter sits beside coin. A farmer settles in rye; the next line is silver; nobody blinks. That mixing is what I want you to see. The hand, by the way, is the founder's throughout — his son never kept these books — the notation is plain and needs no decoding, and you cannot chase these entries into letters, because the correspondence for those years was burned. Just the mixing. Now, the spike of seventeen sixty-eight. The price series built from these ledgers is stark: the rise appears everywhere at once. Coast, uplands, market towns — within days of one another, which for that century is simultaneity. The inland towns did not lead, the ports did not lead, and nothing hopped from town to town; there was no sequence to find. And the partners? At the height, the letters show them carrying. Their ships spent the crisis hauling other houses' grain for freight fees — steady money, no exposure. They never sold out early to watch from shore, timber never tempted them, and the city never engaged them to buy on its account. Carriers, by choice. Which leaves the old story of a merchant ring withholding grain. I dismiss it, on arithmetic alone: no ring could have warehoused enough to move prices beyond a week. The letters give no sign any house held grain back at any stage, the storage registers for those years are lost, and no papers are waiting in a notary's files.
